cor-coordinate-isomorphism.title: The Coordinate Isomorphism
cor-coordinate-isomorphism.html: Let B=(v1,…,vn) be a basis of a vector space V over F. Then the coordinate map V→Fn,v↦[v]B is an isomorphism, with inverse (a1,…,an)↦a1v1+⋯+anvn. In particular, every n-dimensional vector space over F is isomorphic to Fn.

cor-matrix-of-polynomial-of-operator.title: Matrices of Powers and Polynomials
cor-matrix-of-polynomial-of-operator.html: Let B=(v1,…,vn) be a basis of a finite-dimensional space V, let T,S∈L(V), c∈F and p∈F[x]. Then [ST]B=[S]B[T]B, [S+T]B=[S]B+[T]B, [cT]B=c[T]B, [Tk]B=([T]B)k for k∈N, and [p(T)]B=p([T]B).

cor-projection-matrix.title: The matrix of a projection
cor-projection-matrix.html: Let V be finite-dimensional and P∈L(V) a projection with rankP=r. Let (u1,…,ur) be a basis of imP and (w1,…,ws) a basis of kerP. Then B=(u1,…,ur,w1,…,ws) is a basis of V, and [P]B=(Ir000)=diag(1,…,1,0,…,0), with r ones.

cor-rank-nullity-consequences.title: Consequences of Rank–Nullity
cor-rank-nullity-consequences.html:
Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F, and let T:V→W be linear.

  1. T is injective if and only if rankT=dim⁡V.
  2. T is surjective if and only if rankT=dim⁡W.
  3. If dim⁡V>dim⁡W, then T is not injective.
  4. If dim⁡V<dim⁡W, then T is not surjective.
  5. If dim⁡V=dim⁡W, then T is injective ⟺ T is surjective ⟺ T is bijective.

def-change-of-coordinates-matrix.title: Change-of-coordinates matrix
def-change-of-coordinates-matrix.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let B=(v1,…,vn) and C be ordered bases of V. The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is the n×n matrix [id]BC:=[idV]BC, the matrix of the identity map idV:V→V with respect to the input basis B and the output basis C. Its j-th column is [vj]C.

def-coset.title: Coset
def-coset.html: Let U be a subspace of a vector space V, and let v∈V. The coset of U through v is the subset v+U:={v+u:u∈U}⊆V. Any w∈v+U is called a representative of the coset.

def-equivalent-matrices.title: Equivalent matrices
def-equivalent-matrices.html: Let A,B∈Mm×n(F). We say A is equivalent to B if there exist invertible matrices Q∈Mm(F) and P∈Mn(F) such that B=QAP.

def-image.title: Image
def-image.html: Let T:V→W be a linear map over F. The image of T is the subset of the codomain imT:={T(v):v∈V}={w∈W:w=T(v) for some v∈V}⊆W.

def-invertible-linear-map.title: Invertible Linear Map
def-invertible-linear-map.html: Let V and W be vector spaces over F, and let T∈L(V,W). Then T is invertible if there exists a linear map S∈L(W,V) such that ST=idVandTS=idW.

def-isomorphic.title: Isomorphic Spaces
def-isomorphic.html: Vector spaces V and W over F are isomorphic, written V≅W, if there exists an isomorphism V→W.

def-isomorphism.title: Isomorphism
def-isomorphism.html: Let V and W be vector spaces over the same field F. An isomorphism from V to W is an invertible linear map T∈L(V,W); equivalently, by @thm-inverse-is-linear, a bijective linear map.

def-kernel.title: Kernel
def-kernel.html: Let T:V→W be a linear map over F. The kernel of T is the subset of the domain kerT:={v∈V:T(v)=0W}⊆V.

def-linear-transformation.title: Linear Map
def-linear-transformation.html:
Let V and W be vector spaces over the same field F. A function T:V→W is a linear map (or linear transformation) over F if

  1. T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) for all u,v∈V, and
  2. T(cv)=cT(v) for all c∈F and all v∈V.

A linear map T:V→V from a space to itself is also called a linear operator on V. We often write Tv for T(v).

def-matrix-of-linear-map.title: Matrix of a Linear Map
def-matrix-of-linear-map.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F, with ordered bases B=(v1,…,vn) of V and C=(w1,…,wm) of W, and let T∈L(V,W). The matrix of T with respect to B and C is the m×n matrix [T]BC:=([Tv1]C[Tv2]C⋯[Tvn]C)∈Mm×n(F), whose j-th column is the coordinate vector of Tvj with respect to C. Equivalently, its entries aij are the unique scalars with Tvj=a1jw1+a2jw2+⋯+amjwm(j=1,…,n). When V=W and B=C, we write [T]B:=[T]BB and call it the matrix of the operator T with respect to B.

def-nullity.title: Nullity
def-nullity.html: Let T:V→W be a linear map with kerT finite-dimensional. The nullity of T is nullityT:=dim⁡kerT.

def-polynomial-of-operator.title: Powers and Polynomials of an Operator
def-polynomial-of-operator.title_html: Powers and Polynomials of an Operator
def-polynomial-of-operator.html: Let V be a vector space over F and T∈L(V). The powers of T are defined recursively by T0:=idV,Tk+1:=TkT(k∈N). For p=a0+a1x+⋯+aNxN∈F[x], the operator p(T)∈L(V) is p(T):=a0idV+a1T+a2T2+⋯+aNTN.

def-product-of-spaces.title: Product of vector spaces
def-product-of-spaces.html: Let V1,…,Vk be vector spaces over the same field F. Their product (or external direct sum) is the Cartesian product (@def-cartesian-product) V1×⋯×Vk={(v1,…,vk):vi∈Vi for each i}, with addition and scalar multiplication defined entrywise: for a∈F, (v1,…,vk)+(w1,…,wk):=(v1+w1,…,vk+wk),a(v1,…,vk):=(av1,…,avk).

def-projection-operator.title: Projection
def-projection-operator.html: Let V be a vector space over F. An operator P∈L(V) is a projection if P2=P, that is, P(Pv)=Pv for every v∈V.

def-quotient-space.title: Quotient space
def-quotient-space.html: Let U be a subspace of a vector space V over F. The quotient space V/U (read “V modulo U”) is the set of all cosets of U, V/U:={v+U:v∈V}, with the operations (v+U)+(w+U):=(v+w)+U,a(v+U):=av+U(v,w∈V, a∈F). The quotient map is π:V→V/U, π(v)=v+U.

def-rank.title: Rank
def-rank.html: Let T:V→W be a linear map with imT finite-dimensional. The rank of T is rankT:=dim⁡imT.

def-similar-matrices.title: Similar matrices
def-similar-matrices.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F). We say A is similar to B, written A∼B, if there exists an invertible matrix P∈Mn(F) such that B=P−1AP.

def-space-of-linear-maps.title: The space of linear maps
def-space-of-linear-maps.html: Let V and W be vector spaces over the same field F. We write L(V,W) for the set of all linear maps V→W, and L(V):=L(V,V) for the set of linear operators on V (@def-linear-transformation). For S,T∈L(V,W) and c∈F, the sum S+T and the scalar multiple cT are the functions V→W defined by (S+T)(v):=Sv+Tv,(cT)(v):=c(Tv)for every v∈V.

def-trace-operator.title: Trace of an operator
def-trace-operator.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V≥1, and let T∈L(V). The trace of T is trT:=tr[T]B, where B is any basis of V. (For V={0} we set trT=0.)

exm-change-of-coordinates-polynomials.title: Coordinates around the point 1
exm-change-of-coordinates-polynomials.title_html: Coordinates around the point 1
exm-change-of-coordinates-polynomials.html: In R[x]≤2, let B=(1,x,x2) and C=(1,x−1,(x−1)2). Find [id]BC, and use it to write p=2+3x+x2 in powers of x−1.

exm-classify-by-dimension.title: Sorting Spaces by Dimension
exm-classify-by-dimension.html:
Which of the following real vector spaces are isomorphic to each other?

  1. R[x]≤5;
  2. M2×3(R);
  3. the upper triangular matrices in M3(R);
  4. C3, regarded as a vector space over R;
  5. U={p∈R[x]≤6:p(1)=0};
  6. R5.

exm-column-row-factorization.title: A column–row factorization
exm-column-row-factorization.html: Find the column–row factorization of A=(120324143617)∈M3×4(R).

exm-complex-conjugation.html: Let T:C→C, T(z)=z―. Is T linear when C is regarded as a vector space over C? Over R?

exm-constant-function.html: Is T:R→R, T(x)=5, linear?

exm-coordinate-transformation.title_html: Maps Given by Formulas in Coordinates

exm-deter.html: Is there a linear map T:R2→R3 with T(1,0)=(2,3,4),T(1,1)=(3,4,5),T(2,3)=(4,5,6)?

exm-deter-two.title: Recognizing Differentiation
exm-deter-two.html: Show that the differentiation map D:R[x]≤3→R[x]≤2 is the only linear map T:R[x]≤3→R[x]≤2 with T(1)=0,T(x)=1,T(x2)=2x,T(x3)=3x2.

exm-differentiation.title: Differentiation
exm-differentiation.html: Show that D:F[x]→F[x], D(p)=p′, is linear. Show also that D maps F[x]≤n into F[x]≤n−1 for n≥1.

exm-differentiation-integration-one-side.title: One Equation Is Not Enough
exm-differentiation-integration-one-side.html: On R[x], let D be differentiation and J(p):=∫0xp(t)dt, so that J(xk)=xk+1k+1 (@exm-differentiation, @exm-integration). On the sequence space FN, let L(a0,a1,a2,…):=(a1,a2,a3,…) and R(a0,a1,a2,…):=(0,a0,a1,…) be the left and right shifts of @exm-shift. Show that DJ=id and LR=id, but that none of D,J,L,R is invertible.

exm-differentiation-kernel-image.title: Differentiation
exm-differentiation-kernel-image.html: Find the kernel and image of D:R[x]≤3→R[x]≤2, D(p)=p′.

exm-differentiation-nilpotent.title: Differentiation Is Nilpotent
exm-differentiation-nilpotent.html: Let n≥0 and let D∈L(F[x]≤n) be (formal) differentiation (@exm-differentiation), D(a0+a1x+⋯+anxn)=a1+2a2x+⋯+nanxn−1, where kak means ak added to itself k times. Show that Dn+1=0. Show also that Dn≠0 when F=R.

exm-differentiation-rescaled-basis.title: Differentiation with a rescaled basis
exm-differentiation-rescaled-basis.html: Let D:R[x]≤2→R[x]≤2 be differentiation, B=(1,x,x2) and B′=(1,x,12x2). Find [D]B′.

exm-dimension-by-surjective-map.title: Dimension of a Kernel from a Surjective Map
exm-dimension-by-surjective-map.title_html: Dimension of a Kernel from a Surjective Map
exm-dimension-by-surjective-map.html:
Find the dimension of each subspace.

  1. The trace-free matrices U={A∈Mn(F):trA=0} (@exm-trace-free-matrices).
  2. U′={p∈R[x]≤n:∫01p(t)dt=0}.

exm-first-isomorphism.title: Identifying quotients
exm-first-isomorphism.html:
Use the First Isomorphism Theorem to show:

  1. R3/L≅R2, where L=span((1,1,1));
  2. R[x]≤n/U≅R, where U={p:p(0)=0}.

exm-hermite-existence.title: Prescribing Values and Slopes
exm-hermite-existence.html: Show that for all a,b,c,d∈R there is exactly one p∈R[x]≤3 with p(0)=a,p(1)=b,p′(0)=c,p′(1)=d. Hence find the cubic that rises from 0 at x=0 to 1 at x=1 with slope 0 at both ends.

exm-identity.title: Identity Map
exm-identity.html: The identity idV:V→V, v↦v, is linear: idV(u+v)=u+v=idV(u)+idV(v) and idV(cv)=cv=cidV(v).

exm-inclusion.title: Inclusion Map
exm-inclusion.html: If U is a subspace of V, the inclusion ι:U→V, ι(u)=u, is linear, because the operations of U are those of V. Its formula is the identity’s, but its codomain is bigger. For instance R[x]≤2→R[x] is an inclusion.

exm-integration.title: Integration
exm-integration.html: Show that J:R[x]→R[x], J(p)(x)=∫0xp(t)dt, is linear.

exm-integration-kernel-image.title: Integration
exm-integration-kernel-image.html: Find the kernel and image of J:R[x]→R[x], J(p)(x)=∫0xp(t)dt, of @exm-integration.

exm-interpolation-by-counting.title: Interpolation as a Count
exm-interpolation-by-counting.html: Let x0,…,xn∈F be distinct, and define E:F[x]≤n→Fn+1 by E(p)=(p(x0),…,p(xn)). Show that E is bijective, and deduce @thm-interpolation-unique.

exm-invertible-operator-by-kernel.title: Invertibility Without Solving Equations
exm-invertible-operator-by-kernel.html:
1. Let T∈L(R[x]≤2), T(p)=p+xp′. Show that T is invertible and find T−1.
  2. Let V be any vector space and T∈L(V) with T2=T+idV. Show that T is invertible, with T−1=T−idV.

exm-kernel-image-degenerate.title: The Zero Map and the Identity

exm-kernel-image-degenerate.html: Find the kernel and image of the zero map 0:V→W and of the identity idV:V→V.

exm-kernel-image-matrix-map.html: Let A=(12032418−1−21−1)∈M3×4(R). Find bases of kerTA and imTA for TA:R4→R3, and decide whether TA is injective or surjective.

exm-map-from-basis-values.title_html: Finding a Formula from Values on a Basis
exm-map-from-basis-values.html: Show that there is exactly one linear map T:R2→R3 with T(1,1)=(1,2,0),T(1,−1)=(3,0,2), and find T(x,y).

exm-matrix-composition.title: Composition with a Fixed Function
exm-matrix-composition.html: Let X and Y be sets and g:X→Y a function. Show that Cg:FY→FX, Cg(h)=h∘g, is linear. Deduce that R[x]→R[x], p(x)↦p(x+1), is linear.

exm-matrix-of-composition.title: Multiply by x, Then Differentiate
exm-matrix-of-composition.title_html: Multiply by x, Then Differentiate
exm-matrix-of-composition.html: Let S:R[x]≤2→R[x]≤3, S(p)=xp, and D:R[x]≤3→R[x]≤2, D(p)=p′, with the monomial bases E2=(1,x,x2) and E3=(1,x,x2,x3). Compute [DS]E2E2 and [SD]E3E3, both directly and as products.

exm-matrix-of-differentiation.title: Differentiation on Cubic Polynomials
exm-matrix-of-differentiation.html: Let E3=(1,x,x2,x3) and E2=(1,x,x2). Find [D]E3E2 for D:R[x]≤3→R[x]≤2, and [D]E3 for D regarded as an operator on R[x]≤3.

exm-matrix-of-matrix-map.title: Matrix Maps and the Identity
exm-matrix-of-matrix-map.html:
1. Let A∈Mm×n(F), and let En, Em be the standard bases of Fn, Fm. Show that [TA]EnEm=A.
  2. Let B be any basis of an n-dimensional space V. Find [idV]B and the matrix of the zero map V→W for any bases.

exm-matrix-of-reflection.title: A Reflection in Two Bases
exm-matrix-of-reflection.html: Let T:R2→R2 be the reflection across the line y=x, T(x,y)=(y,x). Find [T]E for the standard basis E=(e1,e2), and [T]B for B=(u1,u2) with u1=(1,1) and u2=(1,−1).

exm-matrix-of-transpose.html: Let T:M2(F)→M2(F), T(X)=X⊤, and let E=(E11,E12,E21,E22). Find [T]E.

exm-operator-polynomial-relations.html: With P and R as in @exm-rotation-projection-dont-commute, find non-zero polynomials p and q with p(P)=0 and q(R)=0. Also, for an arbitrary p∈F[x], compute p(idV) and p(Z), where Z∈L(V) is the zero operator.

exm-projection.html: Show that T:R2→R2, T(a1,a2)=(a1,0), is linear.

exm-projection-adapted-basis.title_html: Making a matrix diagonal with a well-chosen basis
exm-projection-adapted-basis.html: Let T:R2→R2, T(x,y)=(2x−y, 2x−y). Find a basis B of R2 such that [T]B is diagonal, and check the answer with @thm-change-of-basis-maps.

exm-projection-kernel-image.title: Projection onto an Axis
exm-projection-kernel-image.html: Find the kernel and image of the projection T:R2→R2, T(a1,a2)=(a1,0), of @exm-projection.

exm-quotient-basis.html: Let U=span((1,1,1))⊆R3. Find a basis of R3/U, and write (2,5,−1)+U in it.

  2. True or false: for all S,T∈L(V), ST=TS. Justify your answer.
  3. Let T∈L(R5,R2) and S∈L(R2,R5). Which of ST, TS are defined, and in which spaces do they lie?
  4. For T∈L(V) and p=4 (a constant polynomial), what is p(T)?
  5. True or false: for all S,T∈L(V), (S+T)2=S2+2ST+T2. Justify your answer.

exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-b1.title: B1: Computing compositions
exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-b1.html:
Let S,T∈L(R2) be given by S(x,y)=(x+y,y) and T(x,y)=(y,x).

  1. Compute ST, TS and 2S−T.
  2. Compute S2 and Sk for every k∈N.
  3. Hence show that (S−id)2=0.

exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-b2.title: B2: Operators that preserve a subspace
exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-b2.title_html: B2: Operators that preserve a subspace
exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-b2.html: Let U be a subspace of V, and let AU:={T∈L(V):Tu∈U for every u∈U}. Prove that AU is a subspace of L(V), that idV∈AU, and that ST∈AU whenever S,T∈AU.

exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-b3.title: B3: A polynomial that kills D
exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-b3.title_html: B3: A polynomial that kills D
exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-b3.html:
Let D∈L(R[x]≤2) be differentiation.

  1. Find a non-zero polynomial p with p(D)=0.
  2. Show that no non-zero polynomial q of degree at most 2 satisfies q(D)=0.
  3. Hence, or otherwise, compute (id+D)3 as a combination of id,D,D2, and evaluate (id+D)3(x2).

exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-c1.title: C1: The Heisenberg relation
exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-c1.html:
Let F be a field, let D∈L(F[x]) be formal differentiation, D(∑kakxk)=∑k≥1kakxk−1 (@exm-differentiation), and let S∈L(F[x]) be multiplication by x, S(p)=xp (the map M of @exm-multiplication-by-x).

  1. Prove that DS−SD=id.
  2. Let T∈L(Fn,Fm). Prove that T=TA, where A∈Mm×n(F) is the matrix with columns Te1,…,Ten.
  3. Now suppose that F has characteristic 0 (@def-characteristic), and let n≥1. Deduce that there are no operators D′,S′∈L(Fn) with D′S′−S′D′=id.
  4. Show that the assumption on the characteristic in (c) cannot be dropped.

Hint: for (c), use (b) and consider traces.

exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-c2.title: C2: Commuting nilpotent operators
exr-algebra-of-linear-maps-c2.html:
Let S,T∈L(V).

  1. Suppose ST=TS. Prove that (S+T)n=∑k=0n(nk)SkTn−k for every n∈N, where (nk)SkTn−k means SkTn−k added to itself (nk) times.
  2. Deduce that if ST=TS, Sa=0 and Tb=0 for some a,b≥1, then (S+T)a+b−1=0.
  3. Show that (b) fails without ST=TS: give nilpotent S,T∈L(R2) such that S+T is not nilpotent.

Hint: for (c), try maps that send one standard basis vector to the other and the other to 0.

exr-change-of-basis-a1.title: A1
exr-change-of-basis-a1.html:
1. Define the change-of-coordinates matrix [id]BC, and say what its columns are.
  2. State the change-of-basis formula for an operator T∈L(V) and bases B,B′, saying exactly which matrix P is.
  3. True or false: [id]BC=[id]CB for all bases B,C of V. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A∼B, then trA=trB and rankA=rankB. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if trA=trB and rankA=rankB, then A∼B. Justify your answer.
  6. Describe the method for recovering the change-of-basis formula without memorizing it.

exr-change-of-basis-b1.title: B1: Change-of-coordinates matrices
exr-change-of-basis-b1.html:
1. In R2, let B=((1,2),(3,5)) and C=((1,1),(1,2)). Find [id]BC. If [v]B=(1,−1), find [v]C, and check your answer by computing v both ways.
  2. In R[x]≤2, let B=(1,x,x2) and C=(1,1+x,1+x+x2). Find [id]CB and [id]BC. Hence find the C-coordinates of 3−x+2x2.

exr-change-of-basis-b2.title: B2: A matrix in a new basis, two ways
exr-change-of-basis-b2.title_html: B2: A matrix in a new basis, two ways
exr-change-of-basis-b2.html:
Let T:R2→R2, T(x,y)=(4x−2y, x+y), and B=((1,1),(2,1)).

  1. Compute [T]B directly from @def-matrix-of-linear-map.
  2. Compute it again with @thm-change-of-basis-maps, starting from the standard matrix.

exr-change-of-basis-b3.title: B3: Similar or not?
exr-change-of-basis-b3.html:
Determine which of the following pairs of real matrices are similar. Justify your answer, either with an invariant or with an explicit invertible P.

  1. (1203) and (1002).
  2. (0100) and (0000).
  3. (1102) and (1002).
  4. (2002) and (2102).
  5. (1111) and (2000).

exr-change-of-basis-c1.title: C1: Matrices similar only to themselves
exr-change-of-basis-c1.title_html: C1: Matrices similar only to themselves
exr-change-of-basis-c1.html:
Let n≥1 and A∈Mn(F).

  1. Prove that A is similar only to itself if and only if A=cIn for some c∈F.
  2. Show that N=(0100) and N⊤=(0010) are similar, and explain the answer in terms of the operator x↦Nx and a reordered basis.

Hint: for (a), use the invertible matrices In+Eij with i≠j.

exr-change-of-basis-c2.title: C2: \A\B and \B\A
exr-change-of-basis-c2.title_html: C2: AB and BA
exr-change-of-basis-c2.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F).

  1. Prove that if A is invertible, then AB∼BA.
  2. Show that (a) fails without the invertibility hypothesis, even though tr(AB)=tr(BA) always holds.

exr-change-of-basis-c3.title: C3: Every non-zero 2 \times 2 matrix with square zero
exr-change-of-basis-c3.title_html: C3: Every non-zero 2×2 matrix with square zero
exr-change-of-basis-c3.html:
Let N∈M2(F) with N≠0 and N2=0, and let T:F2→F2, Tx=Nx.

  1. Explain why there is v∈F2 with Nv≠0, and show that B=(Nv,v) is a basis of F2.
  2. Compute [T]B, and deduce that N∼(0100).
  3. Hence show that (2−41−2)∼(0100) in M2(R), with an explicit P.

exr-isomorphisms-a1.title: A1
exr-isomorphisms-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for T∈L(V,W) to be an isomorphism, and what V≅W means.
  2. True or false: R[x]≤3≅M2(R). Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: if dim⁡V=dim⁡W=5 and T∈L(V,W) is injective, then T is an isomorphism. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: for every vector space V and all S,T∈L(V), ST=idV implies TS=idV. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if V≅W, then every linear map V→W is an isomorphism. Justify your answer.
  6. Which theorem would you use to show that a given operator on a finite-dimensional space is invertible by computing only its kernel?

exr-isomorphisms-b1.title: B1: An explicit isomorphism
exr-isomorphisms-b1.html: Let U={A∈M2(R):A⊤=A} be the space of symmetric 2×2 real matrices. Find an explicit isomorphism U→R[x]≤2, and verify that it is one.

exr-isomorphisms-b2.title: B2: Inverting \id + D
exr-isomorphisms-b2.title_html: B2: Inverting id+D
exr-isomorphisms-b2.html:
Let n≥0, and let T∈L(R[x]≤n), T(p)=p+p′.

  1. Show that T is an isomorphism by computing its kernel.
  2. Show that T−1=∑k=0n(−1)kDk, where D is differentiation.
  3. For n=2, find the polynomial p with p+p′=x2.

Hint: for (b), use the polynomial identity (1+x)∑k=0n(−x)k=1+(−1)nxn+1.

exr-isomorphisms-b3.title: B3: Deciding isomorphism
exr-isomorphisms-b3.html:
Determine which of the following pairs of real vector spaces are isomorphic. Justify your answer.

  1. R4 and M2(R).
  2. R[x]≤3 and {A∈M3(R):A⊤=−A}.
  3. {p∈R[x]≤4:p(2)=0} and R4.
  4. C2 (over R) and R[x]≤3.
  5. The plane {(x,y,z)∈R3:x+y+z=0} and C (over R).

exr-isomorphisms-c1.title: C1: Invertible products
exr-isomorphisms-c1.html:
1. Let V be finite-dimensional and S,T∈L(V). Prove that if ST is invertible, then S and T are both invertible. Deduce that TS is then invertible too.
  2. Show that (a) fails for V=FN: give S,T∈L(FN) with ST invertible but neither S nor T invertible, and TS not invertible.

Hint: for (a), regroup (ST)(ST)−1 and (ST)−1(ST).

exr-isomorphisms-c2.title: C2: A space isomorphic to a proper subspace
exr-isomorphisms-c2.title_html: C2: A space isomorphic to a proper subspace
exr-isomorphisms-c2.html:
1. Let V be finite-dimensional and U a subspace of V with U≅V. Prove that U=V.
  2. Let U={p∈F[x]:p(0)=0}, the polynomials with constant coefficient 0. Show that T:F[x]→U, T(p)=xp, is an isomorphism. Hence (a) fails without finite dimension.

exr-kernel-image-a1.title: A1
exr-kernel-image-a1.html:
1. Define the kernel and the image of a linear map T:V→W. Of which spaces are they subspaces?
  2. State the kernel test for injectivity.
  3. True or false: if T(u)=T(v), then u−v∈kerT. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: for D:R[x]≤3→R[x]≤3, D(p)=p′, we have imD=R[x]≤3. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: for a linear T:V→W and any w∈W, the set {v∈V:T(v)=w} is a subspace of V. Justify your answer.

exr-kernel-image-b1.title: B1: Kernel and Image of a Matrix Map
exr-kernel-image-b1.title_html: B1: Kernel and Image of a Matrix Map
exr-kernel-image-b1.html: Let B=(1−1202−2510011)∈M3×4(R). Find bases of kerTB and imTB. Hence decide whether TB:R4→R3 is injective, and whether it is surjective.

exr-kernel-image-b2.title: B2: Kernels and Images Beyond F^n
exr-kernel-image-b2.title_html: B2: Kernels and Images Beyond Fn
exr-kernel-image-b2.html:
For each map, find a basis of the kernel and a basis of the image, and decide whether the map is injective and whether it is surjective.

  1. T:R[x]≤2→R[x]≤2, T(p)=p′+p.
  2. S:M2(R)→M2(R), S(A)=A−A⊤.

exr-kernel-image-c1.title: C1: Kernels and Images of a Composite
exr-kernel-image-c1.title_html: C1: Kernels and Images of a Composite
exr-kernel-image-c1.html:
Let T:U→V and S:V→W be linear.

  1. Prove that kerT⊆ker(ST) and im(ST)⊆imS.
  2. Give an example, with U=V=W=R2, where kerT≠ker(ST).
  3. Deduce that if ST is injective, then T is injective, and if ST is surjective, then S is surjective.

exr-kernel-image-c2.title: C2: When Is a Composite Injective?
exr-kernel-image-c2.title_html: C2: When Is a Composite Injective?
exr-kernel-image-c2.html: Let T:U→V and S:V→W be linear, and suppose T is injective. Prove that ST is injective if and only if kerS∩imT={0}, that is, if and only if S is injective on imT. Give an example where S is not injective but ST is.

exr-kernel-image-c3.title: C3: Differentiation over \nF_2
exr-kernel-image-c3.title_html: C3: Differentiation over F2
exr-kernel-image-c3.html: Let D:F2[x]≤3→F2[x]≤3 be the formal derivative (@exm-differentiation). Find bases of kerD and imD. Which step of @exm-differentiation-kernel-image fails over F2?

exr-linear-maps-a1.title: A1
exr-linear-maps-a1.html:
1. Define a linear map T:V→W over F.
  2. State the theorem that says a linear map is determined by a basis, including both existence and uniqueness.
  3. True or false: if T:V→W satisfies T(0)=0, then T is linear. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: there is a linear map T:R2→R2 with T(1,1)=(1,0) and T(2,2)=(3,0). Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: complex conjugation C→C is linear over R. Justify your answer.

exr-linear-maps-b1.title: B1: Which Maps Are Linear?
exr-linear-maps-b1.html:
Determine which of the following functions are linear maps over R. Justify your answer.

  1. T:R3→R2, T(x,y,z)=(x−2z, 3y).
  2. T:R2→R2, T(x,y)=(x+1, y).
  3. T:M2(R)→R, T(abcd)=ad−bc.
  4. T:R[x]≤2→R[x]≤3, T(p)=x2p′.
  5. T:R2→R, T(x,y)=xy.
  6. T:RN→RN, T(s0,s1,s2,…)=(s1−s0, s2−s1, s3−s2, …).

exr-linear-maps-b2.title: B2: A Formula from Values on a Basis
exr-linear-maps-b2.title_html: B2: A Formula from Values on a Basis
exr-linear-maps-b2.html:
1. Show that there is exactly one linear map T:R2→R2 with T(2,1)=(1,4) and T(1,1)=(0,3). Hence find T(x,y) and a matrix A with T=TA.
  2. Let S:R[x]≤2→R be linear with S(1)=1, S(1+x)=3 and S(1+x+x2)=6. Find S(a+bx+cx2).

exr-linear-maps-b3.title: B3: Evaluation and Integration
exr-linear-maps-b3.html:
1. Prove that φ:R[x]→R, φ(p)=p(3), is linear.
  2. Prove that ψ:R[x]→R, ψ(p)=∫01p(t)dt, is linear.
  3. Hence find φ(a+bx+cx2) and ψ(a+bx+cx2).

exr-linear-maps-c1.title: C1: Over \nQ, Additivity Is Enough
exr-linear-maps-c1.title_html: C1: Over Q, Additivity Is Enough
exr-linear-maps-c1.html:
Let V and W be vector spaces over Q, and let T:V→W be additive: T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) for all u,v∈V.

  1. Prove that T(nv)=nT(v) for every n∈N and v∈V.
  2. Prove that T(nv)=nT(v) for every n∈Z.
  3. Prove that T(qv)=qT(v) for every q∈Q. Deduce that T is linear.

Hint: for (c), apply (b) to the vector qv.

exr-linear-maps-c2.title: C2: Over \nC, Additivity Is Not Enough
exr-linear-maps-c2.title_html: C2: Over C, Additivity Is Not Enough
exr-linear-maps-c2.html:
1. Give an additive map C→C that is not linear over C, and explain which step of @exr-linear-maps-c1 fails for it.
  2. Let V and W be vector spaces over C. Regarding them also as spaces over R, let T:V→W be linear over R, and suppose T(iv)=iT(v) for all v∈V. Prove that T is linear over C.

exr-matrix-of-a-map-a1.title: A1
exr-matrix-of-a-map-a1.html:
1. Define [T]BC for T∈L(V,W) and ordered bases B of V, C of W.
  2. State the formula relating [Tv]C and [v]B, and the formula for the matrix of a composition.
  3. True or false: the j-th row of [T]BC is [Tvj]C. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: [idV]BC=In for any two bases B, C of an n-dimensional space V. Justify your answer.
  5. What is dim⁡L(R3,R[x]≤2)?

exr-matrix-of-a-map-b1.title: B1: Matrices in given bases
exr-matrix-of-a-map-b1.html:
Find the matrix of each operator in the given basis. (Both maps are linear; you may take this as given.)

  1. T:R[x]≤2→R[x]≤2, T(p)=p(x+1), in E=(1,x,x2).
  2. T:M2(R)→M2(R), T(X)=BX with B=(1234), in E=(E11,E12,E21,E22).

exr-matrix-of-a-map-b2.title: B2: Recovering a map from its matrix
exr-matrix-of-a-map-b2.title_html: B2: Recovering a map from its matrix
exr-matrix-of-a-map-b2.html: Let B=(1,1+x,x2), a basis of R[x]≤2, and let E′ be the standard basis of R2. A linear map T:R[x]≤2→R2 has [T]BE′=(10201−1). Find T(a+bx+cx2). Hence find a basis of kerT.

exr-matrix-of-a-map-b3.title: B3: A composition computed two ways
exr-matrix-of-a-map-b3.title_html: B3: A composition computed two ways
exr-matrix-of-a-map-b3.html: Let T:R[x]≤1→R[x]≤2, T(p)=xp, and S:R[x]≤2→R2, S(p)=(p(0),p(1)). Use the monomial bases and the standard basis of R2. Compute the matrix of ST directly, and again as a product of the matrices of S and T.

exr-matrix-of-a-map-c1.title: C1: Upper triangular matrices and invariant subspaces
exr-matrix-of-a-map-c1.title_html: C1: Upper triangular matrices and invariant subspaces
exr-matrix-of-a-map-c1.html: Let V be finite-dimensional and T∈L(V). A subspace U of V is T-invariant if Tu∈U for every u∈U. Let B=(v1,…,vn) be a basis of V, and for 1≤k≤n let Uk=span(v1,…,vk). Prove that [T]B is upper triangular if and only if every Uk is T-invariant.

exr-matrix-of-a-map-c2.title: C2: Integrating with a matrix
exr-matrix-of-a-map-c2.html:
Let f1(x)=ex, f2(x)=xex, f3(x)=x2ex, and let V=span(f1,f2,f3) inside the real vector space of all functions R→R (@exm-vector-spaces (d)).

  1. Prove that B=(f1,f2,f3) is a basis of V.
  2. Show that differentiation maps V into V, and find [D]B for D∈L(V), D(f)=f′.
  3. Hence show that D is invertible on V, and use ([D]B)−1 to find a function g∈V with g′=x2ex.

Hint: for (a), divide a vanishing combination by ex and count roots.

exr-products-and-quotients-a1.title: A1
exr-products-and-quotients-a1.html:
1. Define the quotient space V/U and its two operations.
  2. State the condition, in terms of v−w, for v+U=w+U.
  3. True or false: V/U is a subspace of V. Justify your answer.
  4. State the First Isomorphism Theorem.
  5. If U is a 2-dimensional subspace of R5, what is dim⁡(R5/U)? What is dim⁡(R5×U)?
  6. What must be checked before the formula (v+U)+(w+U)=(v+w)+U can be used as a definition, and which property of U makes the check work?

exr-products-and-quotients-b1.title: B1: A basis of a quotient of \nR^4
exr-products-and-quotients-b1.title_html: B1: A basis of a quotient of R4
exr-products-and-quotients-b1.html:
Let U=span((1,0,1,0),(0,1,0,1))⊆R4.

  1. Find dim⁡(R4/U) and a basis of R4/U.
  2. Write (3,1,4,1)+U in your basis.
  3. Decide whether (1,2,3,4)+U=(3,4,1,2)+U.

exr-products-and-quotients-b2.title: B2: A map that factors through a quotient
exr-products-and-quotients-b2.title_html: B2: A map that factors through a quotient
exr-products-and-quotients-b2.html:
Let T:R[x]≤2→R2, T(p)=(p(1),p′(1)), and U=span((x−1)2).

  1. Show that U⊆kerT, so that T induces a linear map T¯:R[x]≤2/U→R2 with T¯(p+U)=T(p).
  2. Prove that T¯ is an isomorphism.
  3. Compute T¯(x2+U), and find the coset T¯−1(0,1).

exr-products-and-quotients-b3.title: B3: Matrices modulo scalars
exr-products-and-quotients-b3.html:
Let n≥1 and S={cIn:c∈F}⊆Mn(F).

  1. Show that S is a subspace and find dim⁡(Mn(F)/S).
  2. For n=2, find a basis of M2(F)/S.
  3. Show that A+S=B+S if and only if A−B is a scalar matrix, and decide whether (3105)+S=(1103)+S.

exr-products-and-quotients-c1.title: C1: The dimension formula from isomorphisms
exr-products-and-quotients-c1.title_html: C1: The dimension formula from isomorphisms
exr-products-and-quotients-c1.html:
Let U and W be finite-dimensional subspaces of a vector space V.

  1. Using @thm-second-isomorphism and @thm-dimension-quotient, prove that dim⁡(U+W)=dim⁡U+dim⁡W−dim⁡(U∩W).
  2. Give a second proof: apply Rank–Nullity to the addition map S:U×W→V, S(u,w)=u+w, after showing that u↦(u,−u) is an isomorphism from U∩W onto kerS.

exr-products-and-quotients-c2.title: C2: The operator induced on a quotient
exr-products-and-quotients-c2.title_html: C2: The operator induced on a quotient
exr-products-and-quotients-c2.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional, T∈L(V), and U a subspace with Tu∈U for every u∈U.

  1. Prove that T¯(v+U):=Tv+U is a well-defined linear operator on V/U.
  2. Let (u1,…,um) be a basis of U, extended to a basis B=(u1,…,um,w1,…,ws) of V. Show that [T]B=(AB0D), where A∈Mm(F) is the matrix of the restriction T|U:U→U in (u1,…,um), D∈Ms(F) is the matrix of T¯ in (w1+U,…,ws+U), and 0 is the s×m zero matrix.
  3. Check (b) when T is differentiation on R[x]≤2, with U=R[x]≤1 and B=(1,x,x2).

Hint: for (a), apply @thm-quotient-universal-property to π∘T.

exr-products-and-quotients-c3.title: C3: Counting cosets over a finite field
exr-products-and-quotients-c3.title_html: C3: Counting cosets over a finite field
exr-products-and-quotients-c3.html:
Let F=Fq be a finite field with q elements, V a vector space over F of dimension n, and U a subspace of dimension m.

  1. Show that |V|=qn.
  2. Show that every coset v+U has exactly |U| elements, and deduce |V/U|=qn−m by counting.
  3. Check that (b) agrees with @thm-dimension-quotient.

exr-projections-and-trace-a1.title: A1
exr-projections-and-trace-a1.html:
1. Define a projection P∈L(V), and state the correspondence between projections and direct sum decompositions.
  2. True or false: a projection is determined by its image. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: an operator T on R2 with imT the x-axis and kerT the y-axis is a projection. Justify your answer.
  4. Explain why trT does not depend on the basis used to compute it.
  5. True or false: for every field F and every projection P on a finite-dimensional space over F, the integer rankP can be recovered from trP∈F. Justify your answer.
  6. Where does the hypothesis “characteristic not 2” enter the proof of @thm-involution-decomposition?

exr-projections-and-trace-b1.title: B1: A projection in \nR^3
exr-projections-and-trace-b1.title_html: B1: A projection in R3
exr-projections-and-trace-b1.html:
Let U={(x,y,z)∈R3:x+y−z=0} and L=span((1,1,1)).

  1. Show that R3=U⊕L.
  2. Find the standard matrix A of the projection P onto U along L.
  3. Verify that A2=A, and that trA=rankA.

exr-projections-and-trace-b2.title: B2: The complementary projection
exr-projections-and-trace-b2.html:
Let P∈L(V) be a projection.

  1. Prove that idV−P is a projection.
  2. Prove that im(idV−P)=kerP and ker(idV−P)=imP.
  3. Deduce that if P is the projection onto U along W, then idV−P is the projection onto W along U.

exr-projections-and-trace-b3.title: B3: Traces of operators on matrices
exr-projections-and-trace-b3.title_html: B3: Traces of operators on matrices
exr-projections-and-trace-b3.html:
1. Let τ:Mn(F)→Mn(F), τ(A)=A⊤. Show that trτ=n⋅1.
  2. Fix B∈M2(F), and let LB:M2(F)→M2(F), LB(X)=BX. Show that trLB=2trB.

Hint: use the basis of matrix units Eij.

exr-projections-and-trace-c1.title: C1: When is a sum of projections a projection?
exr-projections-and-trace-c1.title_html: C1: When is a sum of projections a projection?
exr-projections-and-trace-c1.html:
Let F have characteristic not 2, and let P,Q∈L(V) be projections.

  1. Prove that P+Q is a projection if and only if PQ=QP=0.
  2. Show that (a) fails over F2.
  3. Suppose V is finite-dimensional over R and P+Q is a projection. Deduce that rank(P+Q)=rankP+rankQ.

Hint: for (⇒) in (a), use the relation PQ+QP=0 together with P2=P.

exr-projections-and-trace-c2.title: C2: The trace is the only trace-like functional
exr-projections-and-trace-c2.title_html: C2: The trace is the only trace-like functional
exr-projections-and-trace-c2.html:
Let n≥1, and let φ:Mn(F)→F be linear with φ(AB)=φ(BA) for all A,B∈Mn(F).

  1. Using EijEjk=Eik and EjkEij=0 for k≠i, show that φ(Eik)=0 whenever i≠k.
  2. Show that φ(Eii)=φ(Ejj) for all i,j.
  3. Deduce that φ=ctr for some c∈F, and conversely that every ctr has the property.

exr-rank-factorization-a1.title: A1
exr-rank-factorization-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for A,B∈Mm×n(F) to be equivalent.
  2. State the Rank Normal Form theorem for a matrix A∈Mm×n(F).
  3. True or false: equivalent square matrices are similar. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: rank(AB)=rank(BA) for all A,B∈Mn(F). Justify your answer.
  5. How many equivalence classes does M2×5(F7) have?
  6. In the proof of the normal form for T:V→W, which vectors form the end of the basis of V, and which vectors form the start of the basis of W?

exr-rank-factorization-b1.title: B1: A column–row factorization
exr-rank-factorization-b1.html: Find the column–row factorization of A=(1−1202−2511−131)∈M3×4(R). Hence write the second and fourth columns of A as combinations of its pivot columns.

exr-rank-factorization-b2.title: B2: Normal form of a rank-one matrix
exr-rank-factorization-b2.title_html: B2: Normal form of a rank-one matrix
exr-rank-factorization-b2.html: Let A=(1−12−22−4)∈M2×3(R). Find invertible Q∈M2(R) and P∈M3(R) such that QAP=(100000), following the proof of @thm-rank-normal-form.

exr-rank-factorization-b3.title: B3: Rank-one pieces
exr-rank-factorization-b3.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F).

  1. Use @thm-column-row-factorization to show that if rankA=1, then A=xy⊤ for some non-zero x∈Fm and y∈Fn.
  2. Show that if rankA=r≥1, then A is a sum of r matrices of rank 1, and that it is not a sum of fewer than r matrices of rank 1.
  3. Write (120324143617) as a sum of two rank-one matrices.

exr-rank-factorization-c1.title: C1: Frobenius’s rank inequality
exr-rank-factorization-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F), B∈Mn×p(F) and C∈Mp×q(F). Write N=nul(A)⊆Fn, and let S:Fn→Fm be Sy=Ay.

  1. Show that col(AB)={Ay:y∈col(B)}, and deduce from Rank–Nullity for S|col(B) that rank(AB)=rankB−dim⁡(N∩col(B)).
  2. Show similarly that rank(ABC)=rank(BC)−dim⁡(N∩col(BC)).
  3. Prove that col(BC)⊆col(B), and deduce Frobenius’s inequality rank(ABC)+rankB≥rank(AB)+rank(BC).
  4. Deduce Sylvester’s inequality for matrices from (c).

Hint: for (d), look for a special choice of the middle factor.

exr-rank-factorization-c2.title: C2: Counting over \nF_2
exr-rank-factorization-c2.title_html: C2: Counting over F2
exr-rank-factorization-c2.html:
1. Show that M2(F2) contains exactly 1 matrix of rank 0, 6 of rank 2 and 9 of rank 1.
  2. Deduce the sizes of the equivalence classes of M2(F2).
  3. Compare with similarity: how many matrices of M2(F2) are similar to I2? Is the class of I2 under equivalence a union of several similarity classes?

exr-rank-nullity-a1.title: A1
exr-rank-nullity-a1.html:
1. Define the rank and the nullity of a linear map.
  2. State the Rank–Nullity Theorem, with its hypotheses.
  3. True or false: there is an injective linear map R4→R3. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if V is finite-dimensional and T:V→V is linear with imT=V, then T is injective. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: every injective linear map FN→FN is surjective. Justify your answer.
  6. Name the four steps of the proof of Rank–Nullity.

exr-rank-nullity-b1.title: B1: Verifying Rank–Nullity
exr-rank-nullity-b1.html:
For each map, find a basis of the kernel and a basis of the image, and verify that nullityT+rankT=dim⁡V.

  1. TC:R4→R3, where C=(1012011−11121).
  2. T:R[x]≤3→R2, T(p)=(p(0),p(1)).
  3. T:M2(R)→M2(R), T(A)=A+A⊤.

exr-rank-nullity-b2.title: B2: Bijective by the Kernel Alone
exr-rank-nullity-b2.title_html: B2: Bijective by the Kernel Alone
exr-rank-nullity-b2.html:
Let n≥0 and T:R[x]≤n→R[x]≤n, T(p)=p+xp′.

  1. Show that T is a linear map into R[x]≤n and that kerT={0}. Deduce that T is bijective.
  2. Hence show that there is exactly one p∈R[x]≤2 with p+xp′=1+x+x2, and find it.

exr-rank-nullity-b3.title: B3: A Dimension via a Surjective Map
exr-rank-nullity-b3.title_html: B3: A Dimension via a Surjective Map
exr-rank-nullity-b3.html: Let U={p∈R[x]≤4:p(1)=p(2)=0}. Use a surjective linear map to show that dim⁡U=3. Hence find a basis of U.

exr-rank-nullity-c1.title: C1: A Lower Bound for the Rank of a Composite
exr-rank-nullity-c1.title_html: C1: A Lower Bound for the Rank of a Composite
exr-rank-nullity-c1.html:
Let U and V be finite-dimensional, let W be a vector space, all over F, and let T:U→V and S:V→W be linear. Write ST for the composite S∘T, which is linear (see the note before @exr-kernel-image-c1). Let S′:imT→W be the restriction of S to imT, that is, S′(v)=S(v) for v∈imT.

  1. Show that S′ is linear, that imS′=im(ST) and that kerS′=kerS∩imT.
  2. Deduce that rank(ST)=rankT−dim⁡(kerS∩imT).
  3. Hence prove Sylvester’s inequality: rank(ST)≥rankS+rankT−dim⁡V.
  4. Deduce that rank(AB)≥rankA+rankB−n for A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×p(F).

Hint: for (c), compare kerS∩imT with kerS.

exr-rank-nullity-c2.title: C2: When the Kernel Equals the Image
exr-rank-nullity-c2.title_html: C2: When the Kernel Equals the Image
exr-rank-nullity-c2.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional and T:V→V linear with kerT=imT.

  1. Prove that dim⁡V is even.
  2. Give an example of such a T on R2, and one on R4.
  3. Is there such a T on R3? Justify your answer.

lem-coset-equality.title: When two cosets are equal
lem-coset-equality.html:
Let U be a subspace of V. For v,w∈V, write v∼w if v−w∈U.

  1. ∼ is an equivalence relation on V, and the equivalence class of v is the coset v+U.
  2. v+U=w+U if and only if v−w∈U.
  3. Two cosets of U are either equal or disjoint, and every vector of V lies in exactly one coset.

prp-complement-isomorphic-to-quotient.title: A complement is a model of the quotient
prp-complement-isomorphic-to-quotient.title_html: A complement is a model of the quotient
prp-complement-isomorphic-to-quotient.html: Let U be a subspace of V, and let W be a subspace with V=U⊕W. Then the restriction of the quotient map, W→V/U, w↦w+U, is an isomorphism.

prp-invertible-matrix-change-of-basis.title: Invertible matrices are changes of basis
prp-invertible-matrix-change-of-basis.title_html: Invertible matrices are changes of basis
prp-invertible-matrix-change-of-basis.html: Let B=(v1,…,vn) be a basis of V, and let P=(pij)∈Mn(F) be invertible. Put vj′:=p1jv1+p2jv2+⋯+pnjvn(j=1,…,n). Then B′=(v1′,…,vn′) is a basis of V, and [id]B′B=P.

prp-rank-minimal-factorization.title: Rank as the size of the thinnest factorization
prp-rank-minimal-factorization.title_html: Rank as the size of the thinnest factorization
prp-rank-minimal-factorization.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) be non-zero. Then rankA is the smallest integer s≥1 such that A=BD for some B∈Mm×s(F) and D∈Ms×n(F).

prp-similarity-invariants.title: More similarity invariants
prp-similarity-invariants.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) with B=P−1AP for an invertible P.

  1. rankA=rankB.
  2. A is invertible if and only if B is invertible.
  3. For every polynomial p∈F[x], p(B)=P−1p(A)P. In particular, p(A)=0 if and only if p(B)=0; for example, A2=0 if and only if B2=0.

thm-change-of-basis-maps.title: Change of Basis for Linear Maps
thm-change-of-basis-maps.title_html: Change of Basis for Linear Maps
thm-change-of-basis-maps.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F, let B,B′ be bases of V and C,C′ bases of W, and let T:V→W be linear. Then [T]B′C′=[id]CC′[T]BC[id]B′B. In particular, for an operator T∈L(V) and bases B,B′ of V, with P=[id]B′B, [T]B′=P−1[T]BP.

thm-change-of-coordinates.title: Change of Coordinates
thm-change-of-coordinates.html:
Let V be a vector space of dimension n, and let B, C, D be bases of V.

  1. For every v∈V, [v]C=[id]BC[v]B. Moreover, [id]BC is the only matrix M∈Mn(F) with [v]C=M[v]B for every v∈V.
  2. [id]BD=[id]CD[id]BC.
  3. [id]BC is invertible, and ([id]BC)−1=[id]CB.

thm-column-row-factorization.title: Column–Row Factorization
thm-column-row-factorization.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) have rank r≥1, with pivot columns j1<⋯<jr. Let C∈Mm×r(F) be the matrix whose columns are the pivot columns aj1,…,ajr of A, and let R∈Mr×n(F) consist of the first r rows of the reduced row echelon form of A, that is, its non-zero rows. Then A=CR. Moreover, the columns of C are linearly independent and the rows of R are linearly independent.

thm-composition-linear.title: Composition of Linear Maps
thm-composition-linear.html:
Let U,V,W,X be vector spaces over F.

  1. (Linearity) If T∈L(U,V) and S∈L(V,W), then ST∈L(U,W).
  2. (Associativity) If T∈L(U,V), S∈L(V,W) and R∈L(W,X), then R(ST)=(RS)T.
  3. (Identities) If T∈L(U,V), then TidU=T=idVT.
  4. (Distributivity) If T,T1,T2∈L(U,V), S,S1,S2∈L(V,W) and c∈F, then (S1+S2)T=S1T+S2T,S(T1+T2)=ST1+ST2,(cS)T=c(ST)=S(cT).

thm-dimension-of-product.title: Dimension of a Product
thm-dimension-of-product.html: Let V1,…,Vk be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F, and let (bi1,…,bini) be a basis of Vi for each i. Then the list of all vectors ιi(bij), for i=1,…,k and j=1,…,ni, is a basis of V1×⋯×Vk. In particular, dim⁡(V1×⋯×Vk)=dim⁡V1+⋯+dim⁡Vk.

thm-dimension-quotient.title: Dimension of a Quotient
thm-dimension-quotient.html: Let V be finite-dimensional and U a subspace of V. Then V/U is finite-dimensional and dim⁡(V/U)=dim⁡V−dim⁡U. More precisely, if (u1,…,um,w1,…,ws) is a basis of V such that (u1,…,um) is a basis of U, then (w1+U,…,ws+U) is a basis of V/U.

thm-equivalent-condition.title: One-Line Test for Linearity
thm-equivalent-condition.html: Let V and W be vector spaces over F, and let T:V→W be a function. Then T is linear if and only if T(cu+v)=cT(u)+T(v)for all c∈F and all u,v∈V.

thm-first-isomorphism.title: First Isomorphism Theorem
thm-first-isomorphism.html: Let T:V→W be a linear map, and let K=kerT. Then the rule T¯:V/K→W,T¯(v+K)=Tv defines a linear map, which is injective with imT¯=imT, and satisfies T¯∘π=T. Hence V/kerT≅imT.

thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images.title: The Image Is Spanned by the Images of a Spanning List
thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images.title_html: The Image Is Spanned by the Images of a Spanning List
thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images.html: Let T:V→W be linear, and suppose (v1,…,vk) spans V. Then imT=span(T(v1),…,T(vk)). In particular, if V is finite-dimensional, then so is imT, even when W is not.

thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel.title: Kernel Test for Injectivity
thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel.html: Let T:V→W be linear. Then T is injective if and only if kerT={0}.

thm-injective-preserves-independence.title: Injective Maps Preserve Independence, Surjective Maps Preserve Spanning
thm-injective-preserves-independence.title_html: Injective Maps Preserve Independence, Surjective Maps Preserve Spanning
thm-injective-preserves-independence.html:
Let T:V→W be linear.

  1. If T is injective and (v1,…,vk) is linearly independent in V, then (T(v1),…,T(vk)) is linearly independent in W.
  2. If T is surjective and (v1,…,vk) spans V, then (T(v1),…,T(vk)) spans W.
  3. If (v1,…,vn) is a basis of V, then T is injective if and only if (T(v1),…,T(vn)) is linearly independent, and T is surjective if and only if (T(v1),…,T(vn)) spans W.

thm-internal-external-direct-sum.title: Internal and External Direct Sums
thm-internal-external-direct-sum.html:
1. Let U1,…,Uk be subspaces of a vector space V, and let S:U1×⋯×Uk→V,S(u1,…,uk)=u1+⋯+uk. Then S is linear with imS=U1+⋯+Uk. It is injective if and only if the sum U1+⋯+Uk is direct. In that case S is an isomorphism from U1×⋯×Uk onto U1⊕⋯⊕Uk.
  2. Conversely, let V1,…,Vk be vector spaces over F. Then the images ιi(Vi) are subspaces of V1×⋯×Vk, each isomorphic to Vi via ιi, and V1×⋯×Vk=ι1(V1)⊕⋯⊕ιk(Vk).

thm-inverse-is-linear.title: The Inverse of a Linear Bijection Is Linear
thm-inverse-is-linear.title_html: The Inverse of a Linear Bijection Is Linear
thm-inverse-is-linear.html: Let T∈L(V,W) be bijective. Then its inverse function T−1:W→V is linear. Consequently, a linear map T is invertible if and only if it is bijective.

thm-invertible-operator-tfae.title: Invertible Operator Theorem
thm-invertible-operator-tfae.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let T∈L(V). The following are equivalent.

  1. T is invertible.
  2. T is injective.
  3. kerT={0}, that is, nullityT=0.
  4. T is surjective.
  5. rankT=dim⁡V.
  6. There is S∈L(V) with ST=idV.
  7. There is S∈L(V) with TS=idV.
  8. T maps some basis of V to a basis of V.
  9. T maps every basis of V to a basis of V.

thm-involution-decomposition.title: Involutions Split the Space
thm-involution-decomposition.html: Let F be a field of characteristic not 2, V a vector space over F, and T∈L(V) with T2=idV. Then V=E+⊕E−, and the projection onto E+ along E− is 12(idV+T).

thm-isomorphic-equivalence-relation.title: Isomorphism Is an Equivalence Relation
thm-isomorphic-equivalence-relation.html: For vector spaces over F: V≅V; if V≅W then W≅V; and if U≅V and V≅W then U≅W.

thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension.title: Classification of Finite-Dimensional Spaces
thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over the same field F. Then V≅W⟺dim⁡V=dim⁡W.

thm-isomorphism-preserves-bases.title: Isomorphisms Carry Bases to Bases
thm-isomorphism-preserves-bases.html: Let T:V→W be an isomorphism, and let (v1,…,vn) be a basis of V. Then (Tv1,…,Tvn) is a basis of W.

thm-linear-combination.title: Linear Maps Preserve Linear Combinations
thm-linear-combination.html: Let T:V→W be linear, let v1,…,vk∈V and a1,…,ak∈F, where k≥0. Then T(a1v1+⋯+akvk)=a1T(v1)+⋯+akT(vk).

thm-linear-map-from-any-basis.title: Linear Maps on an Arbitrary Basis
thm-linear-map-from-any-basis.title_html: Linear Maps on an Arbitrary Basis
thm-linear-map-from-any-basis.html: Let V and W be vector spaces over F, let B be a basis of V (possibly infinite, in the sense of @thm-basis-extension-general), and for each b∈B let wb∈W be any vector. Then there is exactly one linear map T:V→W with Tb=wb for every b∈B.

thm-linear-maps-isomorphic-to-matrices.title: \cL(V, W) \cong M_{m \times n}(F)
thm-linear-maps-isomorphic-to-matrices.title_html: L(V,W)≅Mm×n(F)
thm-linear-maps-isomorphic-to-matrices.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F with ordered bases B=(v1,…,vn) and C=(w1,…,wm). Then the map Φ:L(V,W)→Mm×n(F),T↦[T]BC, is an isomorphism. In particular, dim⁡L(V,W)=mn=(dim⁡V)(dim⁡W).

thm-linear-maps-vector-space.title: \cL(V, W) Is a Vector Space
thm-linear-maps-vector-space.title_html: L(V,W) Is a Vector Space
thm-linear-maps-vector-space.html: Let V and W be vector spaces over F. If S,T∈L(V,W) and c∈F, then S+T and cT are linear. With the operations of @def-space-of-linear-maps, L(V,W) is a vector space over F. Its zero vector is the zero map v↦0W, and the negative of T is (−1)T:v↦−Tv.

thm-linear-transform-basis.title: Linear Maps Are Determined by a Basis
thm-linear-transform-basis.title_html: Linear Maps Are Determined by a Basis
thm-linear-transform-basis.html: Let V and W be vector spaces over F, let B=(v1,…,vn) be a basis of V, and let w1,…,wn∈W be any vectors. Then there exists exactly one linear map T:V→W such that T(vi)=wifor i=1,…,n. It is given by T(a1v1+⋯+anvn)=a1w1+⋯+anwn for all a1,…,an∈F.

thm-matrix-of-composition.title: Matrix of a Composition
thm-matrix-of-composition.html: Let U,V,W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F with ordered bases B, C, D respectively. Let T∈L(U,V) and S∈L(V,W). Then [ST]BD=[S]CD[T]BC.

thm-matrix-of-map-coordinates.title: Coordinates of an Image
thm-matrix-of-map-coordinates.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F with ordered bases B=(v1,…,vn) and C=(w1,…,wm), and let T∈L(V,W). Then for every v∈V, [Tv]C=[T]BC[v]B. Moreover, [T]BC is the only matrix A∈Mm×n(F) with [Tv]C=A[v]B for all v∈V.

thm-one-sided-inverse-maps.title: One-Sided Inverses of Linear Maps
thm-one-sided-inverse-maps.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F with dim⁡V=dim⁡W. Let T∈L(V,W) and S∈L(W,V). If ST=idV, then TS=idW. In that case T and S are both isomorphisms, S=T−1 and T=S−1.

thm-polynomial-of-operator-properties.title: Polynomials in One Operator
thm-polynomial-of-operator-properties.html:
Let T∈L(V) and p,q∈F[x]. Then:

  1. TjTk=Tj+k for all j,k∈N;
  2. (p+q)(T)=p(T)+q(T) and (pq)(T)=p(T)q(T);
  3. p(T)q(T)=q(T)p(T).

thm-preserves-negation.title: Linear Maps Preserve Negatives
thm-preserves-negation.html: Let T:V→W be linear. Then T(−v)=−T(v) and T(u−v)=T(u)−T(v) for all u,v∈V.

thm-projection-direct-sum.title: Projections and Direct Sums
thm-projection-direct-sum.html:
Let V be a vector space.

  1. If P∈L(V) is a projection, then V=imP⊕kerP, P is the identity on imP, and P is zero on kerP.
  2. Conversely, suppose V=U⊕W. Then there is exactly one operator P∈L(V) with Pu=u for all u∈U and Pw=0 for all w∈W, namely P(u+w)=u. It is a projection, with imP=U and kerP=W. It is called the projection onto U along W.

thm-prop-image.title: The Image Is a Subspace
thm-prop-image.html:
Let T:V→W be linear. Then:

  1. imT is a subspace of W;
  2. T is surjective if and only if imT=W.

thm-prop-kernel.title: The Kernel Is a Subspace
thm-prop-kernel.html: Let T:V→W be linear. Then kerT is a subspace of V.

thm-quotient-space-operations-well-defin.title: The Quotient Space Is a Vector Space
thm-quotient-space-operations-well-defin.title_html: The Quotient Space Is a Vector Space
thm-quotient-space-operations-well-defin.html:
Let U be a subspace of a vector space V over F.

  1. The addition and scalar multiplication in @def-quotient-space are well defined: the right-hand sides depend only on the cosets v+U and w+U, not on the representatives v and w.
  2. With these operations V/U is a vector space over F. Its zero vector is 0+U=U, and the additive inverse of v+U is (−v)+U.
  3. The quotient map π:V→V/U is linear and surjective, and kerπ=U.

thm-quotient-universal-property.title: Universal Property of the Quotient
thm-quotient-universal-property.html:
Let U be a subspace of V, π:V→V/U the quotient map, and T:V→W a linear map.

  1. If U⊆kerT, then there is exactly one linear map T¯:V/U→W with T¯∘π=T, namely T¯(v+U)=Tv. Its image is imT, and it is injective if and only if U=kerT.
  2. Conversely, if some function T¯:V/U→W satisfies T¯∘π=T, then U⊆kerT.

thm-rank-equals-trace-projection.title: Trace of a Projection
thm-rank-equals-trace-projection.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F and P∈L(V) a projection. Then trP=(rankP)⋅1in F. If F has characteristic 0, or characteristic p>dim⁡V, then rankP is determined by trP: it is the unique integer r with 0≤r≤dim⁡V and r⋅1=trP. In particular rankP=trP for projections on real or complex spaces.

thm-rank-map-equals-rank-matrix.title: Rank and Invertibility from the Matrix
thm-rank-map-equals-rank-matrix.title_html: Rank and Invertibility from the Matrix
thm-rank-map-equals-rank-matrix.html:
Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F with ordered bases B and C, let T∈L(V,W), and let A=[T]BC.

  1. The coordinate map v↦[v]B restricts to an isomorphism kerT→nul(A), and the coordinate map w↦[w]C restricts to an isomorphism imT→col(A). Hence rankT=rankAandnullityT=nullityA.
  2. Suppose dim⁡V=dim⁡W. Then T is invertible if and only if A is invertible, and in that case [T−1]CB=A−1.

thm-rank-normal-form.title: Rank Normal Form
thm-rank-normal-form.html:
1. Let V and W be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n and dim⁡W=m, and let T:V→W be linear of rank r. Then there are bases B of V and C of W such that [T]BC=Nr.
  2. Every A∈Mm×n(F) is equivalent to Nr, where r=rankA.
  3. Two matrices A,B∈Mm×n(F) are equivalent if and only if rankA=rankB.

thm-rank-nullity.title: Rank–Nullity Theorem
thm-rank-nullity.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space, let W be any vector space over the same field, and let T:V→W be linear. Then kerT and imT are finite-dimensional, and nullityT+rankT=dim⁡V.

thm-rank-of-composition.title: Rank of a Composition
thm-rank-of-composition.html: Let T:V→W and S:W→U be linear, with V and W finite-dimensional. Then rank(ST)≤min(rankS,rankT).

thm-second-isomorphism.title: Second Isomorphism Theorem
thm-second-isomorphism.html: Let U and W be subspaces of a vector space V. Then U∩W is a subspace of U, W is a subspace of U+W, and U/(U∩W)→(U+W)/W,u+(U∩W)↦u+W is a well-defined isomorphism. Hence (U+W)/W≅U/(U∩W).

thm-similar-iff-same-operator.title: Similar Matrices Represent the Same Operator
thm-similar-iff-same-operator.title_html: Similar Matrices Represent the Same Operator
thm-similar-iff-same-operator.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F).

  1. If V is a vector space of dimension n, T∈L(V), and B,C are bases of V, then [T]B∼[T]C.
  2. Conversely, suppose A∼B. Let V be any vector space of dimension n with a basis B, and let T∈L(V) be an operator with [T]B=A. Then there is a basis C of V with [T]C=B.
  3. Such an operator T in (b) always exists. In particular, A∼B if and only if A and B are the matrices of the operator x↦Ax on Fn in the standard basis and in some basis of Fn, respectively.

thm-sylvester-rank-inequality.title: Sylvester’s Rank Inequality
thm-sylvester-rank-inequality.html: Let T:V→W and S:W→U be linear, with V and W finite-dimensional. Then rank(ST)≥rankS+rankT−dim⁡W. In matrix form: for A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×p(F), rank(AB)≥rankA+rankB−n.

thm-third-isomorphism.title: Third Isomorphism Theorem
thm-third-isomorphism.html: Let U⊆W⊆V be subspaces. Then W/U={w+U:w∈W} is a subspace of V/U, and (V/U)/(W/U)→V/W,(v+U)+W/U↦v+W is a well-defined isomorphism. Hence (V/U)/(W/U)≅V/W.

thm-trace-operator-properties.title: Properties of the Trace of an Operator
thm-trace-operator-properties.title_html: Properties of the Trace of an Operator
thm-trace-operator-properties.html: Let V be finite-dimensional with n=dim⁡V, let S,T∈L(V) and c∈F. Then tr(S+T)=trS+trT,tr(cT)=ctrT,tr(ST)=tr(TS),tridV=n⋅1.

thm-trace-similarity-invariant.title: Trace Is a Similarity Invariant
thm-trace-similarity-invariant.html: If A,B∈Mn(F) are similar, then trA=trB.

thm-zero-maps-to-zero.title: Linear Maps Send Zero to Zero
thm-zero-maps-to-zero.title_html: Linear Maps Send Zero to Zero
thm-zero-maps-to-zero.html: Let T:V→W be linear. Then T(0V)=0W.
